This page goes with **Chapter 21, Augmented Sixth Chords** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AugmentedSixthChords.html). Read each section
there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows the other chromatic chords: secondary dominants
([Chapter 17](secondary-dominants.qmd)) and secondary diminished chords ([Chapter 18](secondary-diminished.qmd)).

Every drill has **Settings**, and is also on the [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page. **▶ Hear it** plays the chord and then where it
goes: to V, or (German sixths) to I64 and then V.

**Typing:** notes with spaces, bass first (`Ab C Eb F#`). Chord symbols as `Ab7`, `Ab7(b5)`, `Ab7(no5)`. The chords' names as `It`, `Fr`,
`Ger`, `EnGer` (with or without `+6`).

## 21.1 Augmented sixth chords

An augmented sixth chord leads to the dominant from both sides at once. **♭6** in the bass falls a half step to 5, and **♯4** above it rises
a half step to 5. The two notes are an **augmented sixth** apart, so they move outward to an octave. In C, that's A♭ and F♯ moving to the
two Gs. In a minor key, ♭6 is already in the key signature, so only ♯4 needs an accidental. These chords do a pre-dominant's job: they come
before V.
[Read 21.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AugmentedSixthIntroduction.html)

## 21.2 The three types

All three start from the same three notes: **♭6, 1 and ♯4**. What's added decides the name:

| Chord | Notes (scale degrees) | In C | In c minor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Italian, **It+6** | ♭6 1 ♯4 (1 is doubled in four parts) | A♭ C F♯ | A♭ C F♯ |
| French, **Fr+6** | ♭6 1 **2** ♯4 | A♭ C D F♯ | A♭ C D F♯ |
| German, **Ger+6** | ♭6 1 **♭3** ♯4 | A♭ C E♭ F♯ | A♭ C E♭ F♯ |
| Enharmonic German, **EnGer+6** | ♭6 1 **♯2** ♯4 | A♭ C D♯ F♯ | (major only) |

The **EnGer+6** sounds the same as the German sixth, but ♭3 is spelled ♯2, because it rises to 3 of a **major I64**. It only occurs in
major keys. The book notes that the national names have no known reason behind them.
[Read 21.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/TypesOfAugmentedSixthChords.html)

## 21.3 Analysing augmented sixth chords

Stack any of these chords in thirds and you find a **diminished third** (A♭ C E♭ F♯ in C becomes F♯ A♭ C E♭, where F♯ to A♭ is a diminished
3rd). No chord met before this chapter has one, so the book's rule is: **a diminished third means an augmented sixth chord**. Then find ♭6 and
♯4, and the remaining note tells you the type.
[Read 21.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AnalyzingAugmentedSixthChords.html)

Name each chord on the staff (keys i, f, g, e):

## 21.4 Lead-sheet symbols

A chord symbol shows root, quality and inversion, not where notes go, and there is no chord symbol with a diminished third. So for
lead-sheet symbols, the book treats each augmented sixth chord as a **dominant seventh on ♭6** whose seventh is misspelled (F♯ for G♭):

- It+6 → **A♭7 (no 5th)**
- Fr+6 → **A♭7(♭5)**
- Ger+6 and EnGer+6 → **A♭7**

That's how the chords are written in jazz and pop, and it matches how they sound.
[Read 21.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/LeadSheetAnalysisOfAugmentedSixthChords.html)

From the name to the symbol:

<div class="drill" data-ex="aug6sym" data-settings="mode=both&most=3&types=It,Fr,Ger,EnGer&dir=find"></div>

And back. A plain 7th chord on ♭6 going to a major I64 can be spelled either way, so both German answers count there:

<div class="drill" data-ex="aug6sym" data-settings="mode=both&most=3&types=It,Fr,Ger,EnGer&dir=name"></div>

## 21.5 Examples

The book's examples, cut where the book cuts them. The popular-music ones (Ellington, Coltrane, Mancini, Fiona Apple, Menken) spell the
chord as a 7th chord on ♭6, as in 21.4. "Friend Like Me" repeats **Am – F7 – E**: i – Ger+6 – V.
[Read 21.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ExamplesWithAugmentedSixthChords.html)

## 21.6 Telling chromatic chords apart

What to look for first, after the book's Table 21.6.1:

| Chord | Look for | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| Secondary dominant | its quality: major triad or 7th chord | V/x, V7/x |
| Secondary diminished | its quality: °, ø7 or °7 | vii°/x, viiø7/x, vii°7/x |
| Mode mixture | lowered notes (borrowed from minor) | iv, ii°, iiø7, ♭VI, … |
| Neapolitan | a major chord on ♭2 | N |
| Augmented sixth | a diminished 3rd when stacked in thirds | It+6, Fr+6, Ger+6, EnGer+6 |
[Read 21.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DistinguishingBetweenChromaticHarmonies.html)

The German sixth and a dominant 7th on ♭6 **sound the same**. Only the spelling tells them apart:
- A♭ C E♭ **F♯** in C is a Ger+6, going to V.
- A♭ C E♭ **G♭** is a dominant 7th, V7 of D♭. D♭ is the Neapolitan in C, so the chord is **V7/N**. (Naming it V7/N is this site's
  addition; the book's chapter on the Neapolitan is [Chapter 20](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Neapolitan.html).)

This drill mixes the two in (key v):

## 21.7 Descending chromatic bass lines

A bass line that falls by half steps from 1 to 5 (**1 – 7 – ♭7 – 6 – ♭6 – 5**) turns up in music of every century since the 1600s, under
many different chords. The book's table lists how each of its examples harmonizes it.
[Read 21.7](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DescendingChromaticBassLines.html)

Here is the harmonization the book lists for Beethoven's 32 Variations in C minor (i – V6 – V42/iv – IV6 – Ger+6 – i64), here with a V – i
added to finish. The voicing is this site's, not Beethoven's:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="60"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:A descending chromatic bass in C minor, with the chords the book lists for Beethoven's WoO 80
M:2/2
L:1/2
Q:1/2=60
%%score {1 2}
V:1 clef=treble
V:2 clef=bass
K:Cm
[V:1] [Gce] [Gdg] | [Gc=eg] [F=Acf] | [^Fce] [Gce] | [G=Bd] [Gce] |]
[V:2] "_i"C, "_V6"=B,, | "_V42/iv"_B,, "_IV6"=A,, | "_Ger+6"_A,, "_i64"G,, | "_V"G,, "_i"C, |]
</script></div>

## 21.8 Chromatic pre-dominant chords

The chapters on chromatic chords add new members to the **pre-dominant** group. Besides IV and ii there are now V/V and vii°/V, the
borrowed iv and iiø7, the Neapolitan N6, and the three augmented sixths.
[Read 21.8](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ChromaticPreDominantChords.html)

Five of them have ♭6 or 4 in the bass, so they are easy to confuse by ear. This drill plays **I – ? – I64 – V – I** and asks for the second
chord. Things to listen for:
- **iv6 and N6** are plain triads.
- **It+6** is thin: only three different notes.
- **Ger+6** sounds like a dominant 7th.
- **Fr+6** has its own colour: all four of its notes belong to one whole-tone scale.

Keys: v, n, i, f, g.

<div class="drill" data-ex="aug6ear" data-settings="mode=minor&most=3&pds=iv6,It,Fr,Ger"></div>

In major and minor, with the Neapolitan too:

<div class="drill" data-ex="aug6ear" data-settings="mode=both&most=4&pds=iv6,N6,It,Fr,Ger"></div>

## For teachers

- **Links with your settings:** open a drill's **Settings**, then **Copy a link with these settings**. Add `&lock=1` for a test, `&count=20` for a score.
- **Chords drilled:** the book's Figure 21.2.1. It+6, Fr+6 and Ger+6 in major and minor; EnGer+6 in major only. Lead-sheet symbols as in
  Figure 21.4.1. The It+6 is shown and asked for with three notes; a written answer with the doubled tonic is accepted.
- **V7/N** (A♭ C E♭ G♭ in C) is the site's addition, for 21.6. It's off except in the 21.6 drill and the last one.
- **Resolution:** ▶ Hear it plays It+6 and Fr+6 to V, Ger+6 and EnGer+6 to I64 then V, and V7/N to N6. The voicings are close position
  above the bass: the drills are for spelling and labelling, not voice leading.
- **The ear drill** voices every chord in four parts in C and moves it to the key. In minor, the tonic chords are minor. The frame
  (I – ? – I64 – V – I) is the same for every answer, so the length gives nothing away.
- **Checked:** `node tests/lessons/aug6-drill.test.js` generates over 10,000 questions and checks each one by its own arithmetic: the
  scale degrees of every note, the augmented 6th, what is drawn against what is played, and which typed answers are accepted or refused.
:::
